newsitem.title: USA: GM to proceed with N.J. cogeneration plant.
newsitem.headline: GM to proceed with N.J. cogeneration plant.

text.p: General Motors Corp is proceeding with construction of a cogeneration plant at its Linden, N.J., truck assembly plant, GM Truck Group said.

The automaker announced a groundbreaking ceremony for the plant after the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities ruled GM did have to pay an exit fee to Public Service Electric & Gas, which had been supplying the plant's electricity.
The board explained it had the right to impose exit fees as a way for utilities to recover stranded costs -- investments made to provide power to the plant that will now supply its own.

In its May 28 decision, the board was acting on the Public Service Enterprise Group Inc subsidiary's September 1996 petition to allow the utility to charge an exit fee to customers using over 500 kilowatts of electricity that cease to take electric service from PSE&G during the board's consideration of utility restructuring.

It also initiated a generic proceeding on exit fees to end consideration on case-by-case basis. Hearings on this proceeding, based on a Bristol-Myers Squibb Co request to buy power from a party other than PSE&G, begin at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT Thursday at the board's offices in Newark.

Thirty minutes later, a few miles away in Linden, GM Truck Group will begin a groundmaking ceremony for the cogeneration plant that will replace its 61-year-old powerhouse, which now supplies the assembly operation with steam and compressed air.

The cogeneration plant will replace all but a megawatt or two of the 24 megawatts of electricity the factory now buys from PSE&G, Kamesh Gupta told Reuters Wednesday. He is manager of strategic planning for utility services in the GM worldwide support group.
He said the cogeneration plant, to be built on the assembly plant site by Quixx Corp, would provide power, steam and compressed air while reducing GM's costs by 20 percent.
"This is a savings today," as opposed to undetermined future savings under retail wheeling, according to John Anderson, director of energy services and supply in the support group.
He said GM assisted Quixx in arranging a natural gas supply for the cogeneration plant but has not been involved in the financing of the plant.

GM spokesman Jeff Kuhlmann said PSE&G had sought an exit fee of $3 million per year to cover its investment in facilities to generate the power GM was currently using and to deliver the electricity to the assembly plant.

The plant will still pay PSE&G a stand-by fee to retain the right to purchase additional power if GM's cogeneration plan develops snags, said Frederick DeSanti, PSE&G's director of state government affiars.

After the board's decision on GM's exit fees, legislation was introduced in the New Jersey Assembly and Senate seeking to prohibit public utilities from imposing exit fees until the Legislature authorizes such fees.

The legislative proposal's statement of intent said it would also prohibit the board from imposing such fees and directs the board to report its findings and recommendations concerning exit fees to state lawmakers and the governor by October 1.
Both DeSanti and his counterpart at GPU Inc, Elizabeth Ard, told Reuters they did not expect the Legislature to enact the proposal.
DeSanti also said he expected an exit fee ruling from the board "in the next 30 to 40 days."
A board spokesman said that would involve a decision on the fees. If the fees are approved, the regulators would then seek a proposal on how to collect the fees.
